modules.title: Fluid Mechanics 1
modules.description: The aims of the ME1 Fluid mechanics course is to establish a strong foundation and understanding of elementary fluid mechanics, on which subsequent courses will build on. Emphasis is on fundamentals. After extablishing the basics of the mathematical description of fluids, fluid statics and dynamics are covered, the latter employing control volume analysis. The knowledge is put to application, particularly in the last part of the course on internal flows.
learningOutcomes: Explain the concept of the continuum description of matter and the description of fluids in terms of fields, and related concepts such as streamlines and pathlines.
Describe in mathematical terms the main forces in fluids, such as pressure, viscous force and gravity.
Solve some basic hydrostatic problems.

Explain and use the equations of continuity, conservation of momentum and conservation of energy, and Reynolds' transport theorem and be able to employ them to derive the conservation laws for a control volume starting from those for a system.
Explain the physical meaning and assumptions of the Bernoulli equation and be able to solve some basic fluid flow problems.
Derive the differential equation for internal flow problems and be able to solve it to obtain the velocity profile.
Explain qualitatively the basic features of turbulent flow.
modules.derivedRationale: Introductory core fluid mechanics covering the mathematical description of fluids, hydrostatics, and fluid dynamics using control volume analysis. It finishes with applications to internal flows and a qualitative look at turbulence. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: fluid-mechanics 0.95 "establish a strong foundation and understanding of elementary fluid mechanics".

modules.title: Thermodynamics 1
modules.description: The principal aim is to give students a basic understanding of the fundamental laws of thermodynamics and the ability to use them in solving a range of simple engineering problems. The pace of the course attempts to take account of students' lack of familiarity with the subject from pre-university studies. The aim of the lectures and tutorials is to develop analytical skills and some design appreciation, involving awareness of the interaction between thermodynamics and considerations of energy resources, materials, solid mechanics, economics, the environment etc.
learningOutcomes: Explain the laws and principles of thermodynamics and the principal thermodynamic properties of steam and ideal substances.
Analyse thermodynamic processes by applying the laws of thermodynamics to systems and control volumes.
Classify a complex thermodynamic process into the main fundamental components.
Solve problems relating to steam and ideal substances undergoing such processes.
modules.derivedRationale: Introduces the fundamental laws of thermodynamics and how to apply them to systems and control volumes, including the properties of steam and ideal substances. It builds analytical problem-solving skills and links thermodynamics to energy resources, materials, economics and the environment. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: thermodynamics-energy 0.95 "fundamental laws of thermodynamics".

modules.title: Mechatronics 1
modules.description: The aim of this module is to introduce Mechatronics as a fundamental concept for modelling and designing machine systems, and to encourage electrical systems to be modelled in a manner compatible with mechanical systems using 'system' concepts; to develop an ability to design, and select components for simple electromechanical systems; to develop mastery of modelling concepts which have direct equivalents in mechanical systems theory, e.g. equivalent characteristics, operating diagrams, complex impedance.
learningOutcomes: Explain the principal characteristics of common electrical components, networks, logic gates, sensors and actuators
Explain the basis on which information is represented and processed electronically in analogue or binary form
Analyse simple electrical networks using Kirchhoff's laws to determine voltage, currents and energy exchanges under d.c. and a.c. excitation
Model a network of sources and impedances as a Thévenin source
Derive, in the form of a truth table, the input-output behaviour of a given network of basic logic gates
Express the structure of a simple analogue or digital network as a circuit diagram, using standard symbols
modules.derivedRationale: Introduces mechatronics as a systems approach to modelling and designing machines, treating electrical circuits in a way compatible with mechanical systems. Covers circuit analysis (Kirchhoff, Thévenin, d.c./a.c., impedance), logic gates, sensors and actuators, and component selection for simple electromechanical systems. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: electronics-embedded 0.80 "develop an ability to design, and select components for simple electromechanical systems"; mathematics-modelling 0.53 "develop mastery of modelling concepts which have direct equivalents in mechanical systems theory".

modules.title: Stress Analysis 1
modules.description: This module introduces the basic concepts and methods of stress analysis. It explains the mathematical descriptions of stress analysis and demonstrates the physical significance of stress and strain and the importance and application of Hooke's Law. We introduce the fundamental concepts of elasticity including Youngs Modulus and Poission ratio. We use these descriptions to show how to solve a range of stress analysis problems including plane frames, stress and strain, pressure vessels and beams.
learningOutcomes: Derive from first principles the mathematical descriptions of stress analysis.
Explain the physical significance of stress and strain and the importance and application of Hooke's Law
Explain the fundamental concepts of elasticity including Youngs Modulus and Poission ratio
Use these descriptions to solve a range of stress analysis problems including plane frames, stress and strain, pressure vessels and beams.
modules.derivedRationale: Introduces the fundamentals of stress analysis, including stress, strain, Hooke's Law and elasticity (Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio). These are applied to problems such as plane frames, pressure vessels and beams. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: solid-mechanics-materials 0.94 "This module introduces the basic concepts and methods of stress analysis.".

modules.title: Materials 1
modules.description: To introduce students to the important mechanical properties that mechanical engineers require knowledge of and to introduce the concept and practice of materials selection. The links between material structure, processing and properties are emphasised. Topics include tensile and fracture properties, material selection, atomic bonding, crystal structure and strengthening. Also included is a focus on the four classes of engineering material: metals, ceramics, polymers and composites, considering the structure, properties and engineering applications of each. Practice in testing of materials is included.
learningOutcomes: Select appropriate materials for common applications, based upon simple selection criteria, and by using Ashby maps.
Describe how selected material properties can be measured and to interpret the common format in which this information is presented.
Explain atomic structure, and types of interatomic bonding and how atoms pack together to form the HCP, FCC and BCC structures.
Explain the difference between elastic and plastic deformation in atomic terms and be able to identify the slip systems in each structure, relating this to brittle or ductile behaviour.
Describe why alloys are used, and how they work, and to draw and interpret an equilibrium phase diagram.
Explain the various ways in which a metal can be strengthened, including non ferrous metals and carbon steels.
Explain the main structural and property differences between metals, ceramics, polymers and composites, the strengths and limitations of each material class and state typical applications of each.
Explain the key issues regarding the sustainability of man's use of materials.
modules.derivedRationale: Introduces the mechanical properties of engineering materials and how to select materials, including Ashby maps. Links atomic bonding, crystal structure, alloying and strengthening to the properties of metals, ceramics, polymers and composites, and covers materials testing and sustainability. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: solid-mechanics-materials 0.95 "Topics include tensile and fracture properties, material selection, atomic bonding, crystal structure and strengthening.".

modules.title: Mathematics and Computing 1
modules.description: This module develops key mathematical and computational skills relevant to the wider mechanical engineering programme. Topics include vector algebra, real analysis, limits, curve sketching, series, applications of integration, complex analysis, functions of more than one variable, matrix algebra, second order ordinary differential equations, and vector calculus . Practical implementation through programming is studied to solve problems selected from the topic areas. These skills are in support of ME1, ME2, ME3 and ME4 modules.
learningOutcomes: Use vector algebra and calculus to solve simple geometric and engineering problems.
Express and manipulate functions of one real variable, two real variables and one complex variable.
Determine the limiting behaviour of functions of one variable, and apply the concept of the limit to differentiation, integration and series expansions.
Sketch functions of one and two variables, including all characteristic features.
Determine Taylor and Fourier series expansions for functions of one variable, by applying the concepts of convergence and orthogonality.
Apply the concept of integration to solve fundamental problems in engineering analysis.
Apply matrix algebra to the solution of systems of linear algebraic equations and eigenvalue problems.
Classify and solve second order ordinary differential equations.
Create python code to implement numerical methods and solve problems selected from the topic areas.
modules.derivedRationale: A core first-year module covering the mathematics underpinning mechanical engineering: vector algebra and calculus, series, complex analysis, multivariable functions, matrix algebra and second order ODEs. Python programming is used to implement numerical methods for problems drawn from these topics. Published assessment: 3 Hour exam (80%, examination), Programming coursework (formative) (4%, coursework), Programming coursework (summative) (16%, coursework). Evidence: mathematics-modelling 0.90 "vector algebra, real analysis, limits, curve sketching, series, applications of integration, complex analysis".

modules.title: Heat Transfer
modules.description: To develop an understanding of the physics of heat transfer and to quantify them. Topics include steady conduction, transient conduction, convection, radiation, and heat exchangers. For all of these topics, practical implementation through solving small design-like problems is studied.
learningOutcomes: Solve simple problems involving heat conduction, convection and radiation for solids and fluids in simple geometries.

Apply design methods to simple engineering calculations on: wall conduction, fins, cooling or heating of bodies immersed in a fluid, transient heat transfer, convection boundary layers and heat exchangers.
Evaluate and explain the significance of dimensionless groups used to characterise heat transfer problems and data.
Translate simple problems involving components, systems and heat exchangers into a form which can be solved using mathematical methods.
Augment and integrate the study of a technical subject, in this case Heat Transfer, by making extensive and efficient use of a comprehensive textbook, such as Incropera’s.
modules.derivedRationale: REVIEW: description is 39 words (under 60), so staff should check these tags. Introduces the physics of heat transfer, covering steady and transient conduction, convection, radiation and heat exchangers. Students solve small design-style problems using dimensionless groups and textbook methods. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: thermodynamics-energy 0.93 "To develop an understanding of the physics of heat transfer and to quantify them.".

modules.title: Stress Analysis 2
modules.description: This course builds on the ME1 Stress Analysis Course by extending the concepts of linear elasticity to two and three dimensions, as the basis for advanced stress analysis. Topics covered include complex stresses and strains, Mohr’s circle, failure criteria, shear stresses in beams, thick-walled cylinders, plastic failure and buckling of struts. The course should enable students to develop sufficient familiarity with stress analysis and strength of materials to design a safe and reliable load-bearing component of simple geometry (or to assess the safety of an existing one).
learningOutcomes: Explain how stresses at a point vary and combine in different directions.
Apply direct stress and shear stress transformation and related equations along with a mathematical understanding of how these equations arise.
Use and explain Mohr's circle to represent complex stresses and strains and solve problems.
Explain how to apply different failure criteria for ductile and brittle materials, along with an appreciation of safety factors.
Solve problems and design components involving stress variations in beams and thick-walled pressure vessels.
Solve problems involving elastic-plastic, fully-plastic bending and residual stress behaviour in beams.
Derive and use Euler buckling theory for different boundary conditions.
modules.derivedRationale: Extends linear elasticity to two and three dimensions for advanced stress analysis, covering stress and strain transformation, Mohr's circle, failure criteria, beam shear stresses, thick-walled cylinders, plastic bending and Euler buckling of struts. It aims to equip students to design or assess safe load-bearing components of simple geometry. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: solid-mechanics-materials 0.95 "extending the concepts of linear elasticity to two and three dimensions".

modules.title: Mathematics and Computing 2
modules.description: This module continues the development of key mathematical and computational skills relevant to the wider mechanical engineering programme. Topics include the analytical solution of partial differential equations, basic numerical methods (interpolation, differentiation, integration), discrete methods for the solution of PDEs (finite difference, finite volume) and the iterative solution of systems of equations. For all of these topics, practical implementation through programming is studied. These skills and techniques are in support of ME2, ME3 and ME4 modules.
learningOutcomes: Solve some simple linear 2D partial differential equations using the method of separation of variables
Employ interpolation in the representation of fields and to write python code to interpolate fields on triangulated 2D domains
Develop finite difference schemes for differential forms of PDE an finite volume schemes for integral forms of PDE
Create python code to solve some simple 2D PDEs using finite difference and finite volume methods
Explain the concepts of convergence and consistency in the context of numerical methods
Create python code for the direct and iterative solution of systems of linear equations
Explain and apply fourier transforms and be able to apply discrete fourier transforms to data using python
modules.derivedRationale: Core second-year module on mathematical and computational methods for mechanical engineering: analytical solution of PDEs, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, finite difference and finite volume schemes, iterative linear solvers and Fourier transforms. Methods are implemented in Python. Published assessment: 2 Hour exam (64%, examination), Computing quizzes (18%, coursework), Computing Final test (18%, coursework). Evidence: mathematics-modelling 0.90 "analytical solution of partial differential equations"; computational-simulation 0.60 "discrete methods for the solution of PDEs (finite difference, finite volume)"; programming-software 0.55 "practical implementation through programming is studied".

modules.title: Mechatronics 2
modules.description: This module aims at building up from basic knowledge of Mechatronics acquired in the first year module, to develop real-life circuits with advanced electronics components. Students will also learn about the fundamentals of Control Theory.
learningOutcomes: Solve basic linear and non-linear circuits by applying the fundamental laws of electronics
Derive electrical equivalents of linear and non-linear circuits
Analyse an analog-to-digital converter and a digital-to-analog converter
Analyse and design circuit elements such as BJT transistor, operational amplifiers and first order passive and active filters
Determine the behaviour of first and second order dynamic systems in the Laplace domain and develop closed loop control systems, with proportional, integral and derivative control
modules.derivedRationale: REVIEW: description is 35 words (under 60), so staff should check these tags. Builds on first-year mechatronics to cover analysis and design of analogue circuits (BJTs, op-amps, filters, ADCs and DACs). Introduces control theory, including Laplace-domain analysis of first and second order systems and PID closed-loop control. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: electronics-embedded 0.63 "develop real-life circuits with advanced electronics components"; control-robotics 0.50 "fundamentals of Control Theory".

modules.title: Materials 2
modules.description: This module develops an understanding, securely based on materials science, of various common failure modes, the reasons for their occurrence and how we seek to avoid failure by design. This module provides the tools and understanding to predict component failures under multiaxial loading conditions due to yielding, fracture, fatigue and creep mechanisms and to identify these failure mechanisms in practice, and to design against them.
learningOutcomes: Explain the basic dislocation behaviours in single crystals and polycrystals
Explain the key strengthening processing in alloys
Explain the common corrosion types and their mechanisms
Discuss, using appropriate terminology, the factors leading to failure of materials and the procedures needed to avoid it
Solve problems involving the prediction of fracture, fatigue and creep failure of engineering materials under multiaxial stress conditions
Correlate possible failure modes with experimental conditions and material properties
modules.derivedRationale: Covers the materials science behind common failure modes, including dislocations, strengthening of alloys and corrosion. It teaches how to predict and design against yielding, fracture, fatigue and creep under multiaxial loading, and how to identify these failures in practice. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: solid-mechanics-materials 0.95 "predict component failures under multiaxial loading conditions due to yielding, fracture, fatigue and creep mechanisms".

modules.title: Thermodynamics 2
modules.description: This module builds on ME1 Thermodynamics to develop an understanding of the principles of a variety of industrially-significant processes concerned with energy conversion and use, and of the design and operation of plant relying on those processes including gas and steam turbines, boilers and heat exchangers, reciprocating engines, refrigeration and air-conditioning plant.
learningOutcomes: Explain the principles of a variety of industrially-significant processes concerned with energy conversion and use
Analyse the design and operation of plant relying on thermodynamic processes
Conduct thermodynamic analyses of the processes involved and select and apply rational performance criteria and parameters.
Explain the constraints on thermodynamic systems imposed by materials, stressing, economics and the environment.
modules.derivedRationale: REVIEW: description is 52 words (under 60), so staff should check these tags. Builds on first-year thermodynamics to analyse energy conversion processes and the design and operation of plant such as gas and steam turbines, boilers, heat exchangers, reciprocating engines, and refrigeration and air-conditioning systems. It covers applying performance criteria and considering constraints from materials, economics and the environment. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: thermodynamics-energy 0.95 "energy conversion and use".

modules.title: Dynamics
modules.description: This module aims to enable students to master the essential basic topics in vibrations and dynamics. Vibration can be a key feature of an engineering system or a source of system failure and this module studies the free vibration of single-degree-of-freedom undamped and damped systems and an introduction to multi-degree-of-freedom systems. In dynamics topics include work-done-energy equation, general plane motion , impulse-linear momentum, angular impulse-angular momentum, impact, generalized angular impulse-angular momentum, simple gyroscopic motion.
learningOutcomes: Derive and explain the dynamical behaviour of one-degree-of-freedom dynamical systems in general terms, using the concepts of natural frequency, damping, free response, forced response, transmissibility, isolation, phasor diagrams and Bode plots
Derive and explain the dynamical behaviour of multi-degree-of-freedom systems in terms of natural frequencies and associated mode shapes, using the concept of modal summation
Explain the concepts of energy-work done, linear momentum-linear impulse, angular momentum-angular impulse and simple gyroscopic motion
Model relatively simple engineering structures as single- and two-degree-of-freedom systems with translational and rotational co-ordinates
Determine the dynamic response of such systems for free and forced vibration
Solve dynamics problems using the concepts of linear impulse-linear momentum and angular impulse-angular momentum
modules.derivedRationale: Covers vibrations of single- and introductory multi-degree-of-freedom systems (natural frequency, damping, forced response, mode shapes) and rigid-body dynamics including work-energy, impulse-momentum, angular momentum, impact and simple gyroscopic motion. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: mathematics-modelling 0.70 "free vibration of single-degree-of-freedom undamped and damped systems"; solid-mechanics-materials 0.50 "work-done-energy equation, general plane motion".

modules.title: Fluid Mechanics 2
modules.description: The ME2 Fluid Mechanics module aims to continue the development of key aspects of engineering fluid mechanics. Topics include dimensional analysis, the mass-conservation and momentum-balance principles applied to a fluid particle, the differential form of the governing equations (Navier-Stokes), incompressible flows, exact (Couette-Poiseuille flows) and approximate (boundary layers, Blasius solution, lubrication) solutions, turbulent channel/pipe flows and the time-averaged governing equations (RANS), compressible flows (speed of sound, Mach cone, isentropic-flow relations and converging-diverging nozzles).
learningOutcomes: Select appropriate dimensionless groups and solve scaling problems
Select an equation of motion, such as Euler, isentropic flow, Cauchy, Navier-Stokes, as appropriate to solve a problem
Simplify and/or approximate the equations of motion to aid solution
Apply appropriate boundary conditions and solve the equations
Evaluate the forces exerted by a fluid on its boundaries"
Explain, in terms of dimensionless groups, the requirements for complete and incomplete similarity between model (e.g. wind tunnel) and prototype flows
Explain the origins and nature of lift and drag relevant to aero- and hydro-dynamic design of transport vehicles
Solve fluid mechanics problems using the force-momentum equation in integral and differential forms
Derive — using an Eulerian control volume — the equations of continuity for special cases (e.g. boundary layer flow) in both Cartesian and cylindrical polar coordinates
Solve fluid mechanics problems describing one-dimensional compressible flow nozzles and diffusers
modules.derivedRationale: Continues core engineering fluid mechanics: dimensional analysis, conservation of mass and momentum, and the Navier-Stokes equations with exact and approximate solutions (Couette-Poiseuille flow, boundary layers, lubrication). It also covers turbulent pipe and channel flow with RANS, and compressible flow including nozzles and isentropic relations. Published assessment: 1.5 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: fluid-mechanics 0.95 "the differential form of the governing equations (Navier-Stokes)"; mathematics-modelling 0.53 "dimensional analysis, the mass-conservation and momentum-balance principles applied to a fluid particle".

modules.title: Design, Make and Test Project
modules.description: This module will be one of the most important in your degree course. Firstly, it aims to reinforce and integrate the knowledge, understanding and skills that you have acquired in engineering science, design, manufacturing and management modules. Secondly - and just as importantly - it sets you to work in a realistic engineering project environment, with rigorous time and budget constraints. When you begin to apply for a job, employers will take your engineering knowledge and analytical skills for granted. It's your team-working and organisational skills which they will need to be convinced of and will set out to test in 'assessment centres'. As part of this module, therefore, Assessment Centre Skills Workshops are offered to raise your awareness of the broader, transferable skills it can help you acquire.
learningOutcomes: Derive and explore the relationship between customer requirements and engineering attributes
Design machine systems and select elements to meet specified objectives
Analyse a given design formally, against specified requirements, and refine it appropriately
Prepare appropriate formal Quality Plan, Budget, Health & Safety and Test plans for a small engineering project
Realise the manufacture of their design using appropriate engineering drawings and appropriate resources
Exercise the key skills needed for team working on a realistic Design, Make and Test project
Record and evaluate progress and decisions in a clear and accurate manner using a logbook
modules.derivedRationale: A core team-based project in which students design, manufacture and test a machine system under realistic time and budget constraints, integrating earlier engineering science, design and management learning. It includes quality, budget, health and safety and test planning, logbook keeping, and workshops on assessment-centre and teamworking skills. Evidence: design-manufacturing 0.90 "engineering science, design, manufacturing and management modules"; management-leadership 0.52 "team-working and organisational skills".

modules.title: Professional Engineering Skills 3
modules.description: This module is comprised of two parts: (a) Engineering in a commercial environment which aims to provide an awareness and basic understanding of some of the non-engineering aspects that will be encountered by professional engineers working in a professional environment. The main topics include: engineering finance; project management;ethics; sustainability; security; professional responsibillity and intellectual property. (b) A literature research project which aims to develop efficient use of the extensive facilities available for research on a given subject, to develop a critical attitude to information sources, an ethical attitude to attributing them and a systematic method for citing them and to stimulate interest in a given engineering-related, technical subject by studying it in depth.
learningOutcomes: Explain the importance of ethical standards and be able to discuss some example ethical situations.
Explain the principles of sustainability and methods for applying them in practical situations.
Choose and apply appropriate tools to the management of projects and project teams.
Justify and apply different methods for assessing the financial implications of decisions and projects.
Explain the importance of intellectual property and methods for its protection and exploitation.
Explain the importance of physical and electronic security, especially of data, and methods to implement it.
Critique the overall state of knowledge on a topic of direct relevance to mechanical engineering.
Summarise the ideas of others in original language and with full attribution in standard (e.g. Harvard) form.
Differentiate between literature of reliable and unreliable provenance.

Synthesise information from a wide range of sources, selecting key information to arrive at appropriate conclusions on a technical subject of relevance to Mechanical Engineering into a coherent written review.
modules.derivedRationale: Introduces the non-technical side of professional engineering: finance, project management, ethics, sustainability, security, professional responsibility and intellectual property. Students also complete an individual literature research project on a mechanical engineering topic, practising critical source evaluation and correct citation. Published assessment: 3 Hour exam (50%, examination), Literature Research Project (50%, coursework). Evidence: management-leadership 0.57 "project management"; finance-economics 0.52 "engineering finance"; policy-ethics 0.52 "ethics".

modules.title: Machine Dynamics and Vibrations A
modules.description: This module aims to enable students to evaluate the dynamic response requirements of a proposed machine design and to produce workable proposals for its safe and effective operation. It will build on the second year Mechatronics and Solid Mechanics modules, introducing a greater range of examples where the dynamic response of a machine must be controlled and making the link between vibration and fatigue failure. This will involve some new subject matter in the vibration of continuous systems, rotor dynamics, signal processing and control analysis. A key aspect of the module is to demonstrate practical vibration measurements and to compare them to solutions of an idealised system in MATLAB. They will also deal with realistic problems involving the assessment of the fatigue life of structures subject to vibration and static loading.
learningOutcomes: Describe simple mechanical systems as lumped parameter models and derive their equations of motion (EOM)
Predict the natural frequencies and mode shapes of multi-degree of freedom (MDOF) vibration systems and of bending, torsion and axial vibration of simple continuous systems such as beams
Explain the importance of avoiding shaft whirl and be able to calculate critical speeds
Explain the significance of vibration loading in generating high cycle fatigue
Predict fatigue life of components by linking their vibration response to alternating stress and using this as input to fatigue calculations
Use MATLAB to obtain solutions to MDOF vibration problems
Use Fourier analysis to convert both single and dual channel time domain measurements in the frequency domain
modules.derivedRationale: Covers vibration of lumped and continuous mechanical systems, rotor dynamics and critical speeds, and Fourier-based signal analysis of measurements. Links vibration response to alternating stress to predict high-cycle fatigue life, using MATLAB to solve multi-degree-of-freedom problems and compare with practical measurements. Published assessment: 3 Hour exam (80%, examination), MATLAB exercise (20%, coursework). Evidence: mathematics-modelling 0.70 "in the vibration of continuous systems, rotor dynamics, signal processing and control analysis"; solid-mechanics-materials 0.60 "the assessment of the fatigue life of structures subject to vibration and static loading".

modules.title: Fracture Mechanics A
modules.description: Fracture mechanics concerns the design and analysis of structures which contain cracks or defects/flaws. Fracture mechanics answers questions such as: What is the largest sized crack that a structure can contain or the largest load the structure can bear for failure to be avoided? How long before a crack which was safe becomes unsafe? What material should be used in a certain application to ensure safety?
learningOutcomes: Explain the foundations, principles, application and limitations (both qualitative and quantitative) of linear elastic fracture mechanics, using appropriate terminology
Explain the micro-mechanisms of crack tip failure in metals, ceramics, polymers and fibre composite materials
Calculate the fracture toughness or fracture energy of a given material from data measured using a standard or well-defined specimen geometry
Formulate problems involving the static, fatigue or impact loading of flawed structures in terms of fracture mechanics
Predict - using fracture mechanics analysis - the residual strength or service live of a flawed structure or the critical size of a defect contained within
modules.derivedRationale: Covers the analysis and design of structures containing cracks or flaws using linear elastic fracture mechanics. Topics include crack-tip failure micro-mechanisms in various materials, fracture toughness measurement, and predicting critical flaw size, residual strength and service life under static, fatigue or impact loading. Published assessment: 3 Hour exam (100%, examination). Evidence: solid-mechanics-materials 0.95 "Fracture mechanics concerns the design and analysis of structures which contain cracks or defects/flaws".

modules.title: Introduction to Nuclear Energy A
modules.description: This module aims provide a basic introduction to the engineering, safety, socio-economic context and prospects for nuclear energy. This module also provides the basic knowledge necessary for more advanced nuclear modules.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a broad understanding of the issues surrounding the use of nuclear energy.
Explain the course that nuclear power development has taken, and its present position.
Explain the underlying physical basis of the generation of energy from nuclear processes.
Explain the main engineering issues in capturing this energy and using it to generate electricity.
Perform basic reactor physics and thermal hydraulic calculations

It includes basic reactor physics and thermal hydraulic calculations and prepares students for more advanced nuclear modules. Published assessment: 3 Hour exam (100%, examination). modules.description: An advanced fluid mechanics module, general and fundamental in nature and spanning subsonic, transonic and supersonic flows. Topics include derivation of conservation equations for incompressible and compressible flows, methods for solving them in simplified cases, turbulence, energy and work and normal and oblique shocks.

Describe the physical features of turbulence, and the basis for models of it
Derive the fundamental differential conservation equation of mass
Manipulate the tensor forms of the conservation equations of mass, momentum energy and energy
Simplify the fundamental differential conservation equations with appropriate assumptions and find, where appropriate, an exact solution
Identify the dimensionless groups that determine the behaviour of fluid flow from the fundamental differential conservation equations
Describe the fundamental features of fluid flow from an analysis of numerical solutions

modules.title: Finite Element Analysis and Applications A
modules.description: The aim of the module is to teach the students to be able to use Finite Element programs in a practical way to solve problems in linear elastic stress analysis. A student who has studied the module should be able, in a later industrial setting, to undertake the analysis of real problems with a fair understanding of sensible modelling procedures. In support of this, the module is split into two stages: (1) Theoretical study of the Finite Element method, with emphasis on understanding what goes on inside a typical, modern, commercial program; (2) Practical experience in analysis using an industry-standard, interactive, Finite Element program.
learningOutcomes: Explain the basic theoretical principles of the Finite Element Method,
Employ industry standard software for interactive FE model generation, analysis and post processing of results.
Interpret the output from this software critically and intelligently in order to yield the required information,
Formulate the boundary conditions of a problem in a suitable form for correct analysis
Assess alternative strategies (of element type, mesh design, boundary condition defintion etc) for economical and accurate FE modelling of specific 2D, 3D and axisymmetric structural problems.
modules.derivedRationale: Teaches the theory of the finite element method and how commercial FE programs work internally. Students then gain hands-on experience using an industry-standard FE package for linear elastic stress analysis of 2D, 3D and axisymmetric problems. Published assessment: 2 Hour exam (80%, examination), 4 small task reports (20%, coursework). Evidence: computational-simulation 0.90 "use Finite Element programs in a practical way to solve problems in linear elastic stress analysis"; solid-mechanics-materials 0.60 "linear elastic stress analysis"; mathematics-modelling 0.50 "Theoretical study of the Finite Element method".

modules.title: Embedded C for Microcontrollers A
modules.description: This module aims to introduce students who are proficient in MATLAB programming to the C programming language: amongst the most widely-used ever amongst programming languages, and one which provides an excellent foundation for learning others (e.g. C++ and JavaScript). It also aims to develop, from the basic knowledge of mechatronics provided in ME2, an ability to build mechatronic systems containing typical sensors and actuators that are controlled by a microcontroller programmed in C.
learningOutcomes: Explain the principal components of, and terminology used in, embedded computer hardware and software
Write simple C programs to manipulate numerical bit-pattern data and text, perform calculations and interface with external hardware
Design, make, test and document a functional mechatronic system containing an embedded microcontroller

modules.title: Mathematics A
modules.description: The ME1 and ME2 mathematics and computing modules focus on predominantly linear systems. The main aim of this module is to show how mathematics can be used to characterise and model the qualitative behaviour of a non-linear systems without solving in detail the equations controlling the evolution of the system. We use the technique of phase-plane analysis to analyze the behaviour of coupled sets of autonomous differential equations and travelling wave solutions of partial differential equations. We use the techniques of Fourier transforms and generalized function theory to analyze the energy and power of signals. We also use double Fourier transforms to investigate the solutions of some partial differential equations. Finally we introduce the ideas of chaotic systems via a study of one-dimensional maps, looking in detail at the phenomenon of period-doubling. Throughout the module the ideas are illustrated using examples relevant to Mechanical engineers, including the simple pendulum and harmonic oscillator.

modules.title: Tribology A

Instead the Tribology module focuses on those areas of Tribology particularly relevant to the design and performance of lubricated machine components. learningOutcomes: Discuss - making appropriate use of technical terminology - the main laws and concepts of tribology and their historical development

We will pay particular attention to the actions of firms and individuals in the context of market interaction and strategic (game theoretic) interactions in business contexts.

It focuses on market interaction and strategic, game-theoretic behaviour of firms and individuals in business settings. Evidence: finance-economics 0.90 "Economics provides a useful set of tools for analysing the world and aiding decision-making by businesses and governments.".

modules.title: Entrepreneurship
modules.description: Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying and exploiting a new business opportunity. An entrepreneur must understand the competitive landscape, estimate the potential demand for their products or services, assess risks and returns, and develop and execute the possible ways to deliver their claims to the best set of consumers. The entrepreneur also needs to acquire resources (funding), compile a team, and generate a vision for the fledgling enterprise.
modules.derivedRationale: Introduces the process of identifying and exploiting a new business opportunity, including understanding competition, estimating demand, assessing risk and return, raising funding, building a team and setting a vision for a new venture. Evidence: entrepreneurship-innovation 0.93 "Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying and exploiting a new business opportunity.".

modules.title: Finance & Financial Management
modules.description: The aim of this module is to enable students to understand of of the core purposed of finance: the setting of prices in a market. The first half of the course works at a market-level, dealing with risk-management and diversification. The second half of the course works at the security-level, thinking about bond, stock, and derivative valuation.
modules.derivedRationale: REVIEW: description is 57 words (under 60), so staff should check these tags. Introduces the core purpose of finance, how prices are set in markets. The first half covers market-level risk management and diversification, and the second half covers valuation of bonds, stocks and derivatives. Evidence: finance-economics 0.94 "the setting of prices in a market".

modules.title: Technologies to Combat Climate Change
modules.description: This module will enable you to appreciate the challenge posed by climate change, and the technologies and systems that will be required to mitigate it. This will be achieved by introducing you to key mitigation technologies and giving you skills to perform basic economic analysis of the options. Lectures will also cover technoeconomic assessment and emissions estimation methods, possible future technology developments and approaches to systems thinking, as well as the policy background on climate change. You will learn about the technologies and systems for combating climate change and calculate performance metrics for these technologies. The module will also teach you how energy systems are interconnected, and how interdisciplinary approaches are needed to combat climate change. On completion of the course, you will be able to develop and analyse technical approaches to tackle climate change, while considering policy, regulatory, and social aspects.
learningOutcomes: List and describe the key functions of technologies and systems that can be used to combat climate change.
Calculate key economic and environmental performance metrics for technologies that can combat climate change.
Describe how energy systems are interconnected, and how changes in one part of the system influence other parts across technical, economic and social aspects.
Analyse, understand and critique approaches to combatting climate change from a range of disciplinary backgrounds.
Plan holistic approaches to combating climate change, undertaking a robust techno-economic assessment and communicate this plan to a diverse audience in a convincing and inclusive manner.
modules.derivedRationale: An introductory module on the technologies and systems used to mitigate climate change, with basic techno-economic assessment, emissions estimation and performance metric calculations. It also covers systems thinking, interconnected energy systems and the policy, regulatory and social context. Published assessment: Online Quiz - individual assessment (10%, coursework), Debate/Presentation - group assessment (90%, practical). Evidence: sustainability-climate 0.90 "the technologies and systems that will be required to mitigate it"; thermodynamics-energy 0.55 "how energy systems are interconnected"; finance-economics 0.50 "basic economic analysis of the options".

modules.title: The Science of Crowds: Movement, Behaviour and Design
modules.description: Why do crowds move in the way that they do? Can we predict this behaviour? Will this change during emergencies such as fires or terrorist attacks? Crowd science - also known as 'pedestrian dynamics' - is able to answer these questions by combining concepts from maths, physics, engineering and design, computing, sociology and psychology. In this module you will be introduced to the basic principles of pedestrian dynamics, such as crowd movement theory, computer modelling, human behaviour, and experimental design. You will also work on a group project, using pedestrian dynamics principles to develop solutions to a real-word design problem. The course will be provided through online video and face-to-face workshops.
learningOutcomes: Define the topics of pedestrian and evacuation dynamics, and explain how these concepts are important to consider when designing infrastructure.
Identify the main emergent properties of crowd behaviour.
Describe the main theories of human behaviour in emergencies.
Explain the different algorithms used for pedestrian dynamics simulation models, including their advantages and disadvantages.
Evaluate the design of pedestrian dynamics and evacuation experiments.
Generate pedestrian dynamics based design solutions for real-world problems.
Communicate design solutions effectively to scientifically literate, multidisciplinary audiences.
modules.derivedRationale: An interdisciplinary introduction to pedestrian and evacuation dynamics, covering crowd movement theory, simulation algorithms, human behaviour in emergencies and experimental design. Students apply these ideas in a group project to solve a real-world infrastructure design problem. Published assessment: Quizzes based on lecture material (20%, coursework), Group project (20%, coursework), Reflective account (5%, coursework), Test after VR session (10%, coursework), Attendance and contribution (10%, practical), Presentation of Group project (35%, practical). Evidence: psychology-behaviour 0.60 "human behaviour"; computational-simulation 0.55 "computer modelling".

modules.title: Innovation, Communication and Teamwork across Disciplines
modules.description: This I-Explore module invites students to work in multidisciplinary teams with peers from across Imperial College London to tackle open-ended, real-world challenges. Whether rooted in health, sustainability, technology, or social impact, these challenges are framed and developed into strategic, well-communicated proposals. Over ten weeks, students progress through the core stages of concept development—defining the problem, understanding user and system dynamics, refining solutions, and communicating their work through two key outputs: a live, in-class pitch deck presentation and a 1-minute video optimised for public or online audiences. No prior experience in design or media is required; students are supported through collaborative workshops and guided feedback. These skills are developed progressively through structured activities and peer interaction, helping students build clarity, confidence, and presence. The module is designed to help students build core skills in framing innovation, working across disciplinary boundaries, and communicating ideas with purpose. These are relevant for any future pathway—academic, professional, or entrepreneurial. Past cohorts have shown strong engagement, with A/B-level performance and over 92% attendance, reflecting the module’s energy and collaborative learning culture.
learningOutcomes: Students will learn how to identify opportunities for innovation, understand stakeholder perspectives, and develop user-centred proposals. They will apply behavioural and design thinking methods to shape interventions and communicate their ideas with clarity and impact. Particular emphasis is placed on both verbal and visual presentation skills—preparing students to engage confidently with a range of future collaborators and professional stakeholders.
modules.derivedRationale: A ten-week interdisciplinary I-Explore module where mixed teams frame open-ended real-world challenges and develop them into user-centred innovation proposals. Students practise design thinking and behavioural methods and communicate through a live pitch and a 1-minute video. Published assessment: Pitch deck presentation (30%, coursework), 1-minute video (30%, coursework), Peer Assessment of other groups’ project videos (20%, coursework), Tutor reports of student participation and engagement (20%, coursework). Evidence: entrepreneurship-innovation 0.60 "core stages of concept development—defining the problem, understanding user and system dynamics, refining solutions"; communication-writing 0.70 "communicating their work through two key outputs: a live, in-class pitch deck presentation and a 1-minute video optimised for public or online audiences".

modules.title: An Accessible Introduction to Quantum Technologies
modules.description: Quantum technologies will drive the next major technological revolution. This module combines interdisciplinary technical knowledge with insights into the broader implications of quantum advancements. You will gain an accessible introduction to the phenomena that underpin quantum computation, imaging, and sensing, and understand the differences between classical and quantum physics. We'll review global initiatives like the UK's National Quantum Strategy, discuss ethical and regulatory considerations, and examine the challenges associated with commercialising deep technologies. By the end of the module, you will be able to discern whether reports of quantum technology represent hype or reality. You will have enhanced your skills in collaboration, public speaking and critical analysis, ready to tackle the future shaped by quantum innovation.
learningOutcomes: Explain how concepts from quantum science enable a range of different technologies (e.g. computing, sensing, imaging).
Describe the opportunities and applications of quantum technologies, and the size/scale of the global quantum ecosystem.
Assess national and international importance of QTs for the economy, national security and wider society.
Outline the challenges of realising robust and resilient quantum technologies, including any ethical implications.
Reflect how your own expertise can contribute to technological development, and the interdisciplinary skills required for quantum careers.
Critically compare alternate, unconventional approaches to computing and sensing, and debate whether quantum offers a technological leap or too much hype.
modules.derivedRationale: An accessible, non-mathematical introduction to the phenomena behind quantum computing, imaging and sensing, and how they differ from classical physics. It also covers national quantum strategy, ethics and regulation, and the challenges of commercialising deep technologies, with a focus on separating hype from reality. Published assessment: Group presentation (25%, coursework), Debate (40%, coursework), Reflective journal (35%, coursework). Evidence: policy-ethics 0.52 "discuss ethical and regulatory considerations".

modules.title: Demystifying Machine Learning: Theory and Applications
modules.description: What is Machine Learning really? And how can it be applicable to you and others around you? This module aims to provide you with an intuitive understanding of the foundations of Machine Learning and how it can be applied to different disciplines. Besides learning the theory behind basic Machine Learning concepts, you will also apply what you have learnt to identify a user problem that can potentially be solved using Machine Learning and deliver a proof of concept of your proposed solution. By the end of the module, you will be able to cut through the Machine Learning hype in the mass media and explain to others what Machine Learning really is all about! You will learn about the dynamics of machine learning and the different learning systems that this technology employs. You will look at this topic through two lenses; theory and application. You will work both independently and in a group setting and utilize your presentation and research skills.
learningOutcomes: Describe core machine learning principles, models and algorithms.
Explain basic machine learning concepts to different audiences, such as laypeople, domain experts, and those with a more technical background.
Identify problems and opportunities in multiple disciplines, including your own, that might benefit from machine learning.
Apply machine learning principles and algorithms to solve a problem in an applied discipline, and critically evaluate other people’s solutions.
Reflect on how machine learning is applicable to you at a personal level, within your surrounding context and the wider context.
modules.derivedRationale: An introductory, accessible module on the foundations of machine learning, covering core concepts, models and algorithms and how they apply across disciplines. Students identify a user problem, pitch it and build a proof-of-concept ML solution, while practising explaining ML to different audiences. Published assessment: Self-reflection document (10%, coursework), Project Milestone 1: Pitch (15%, practical), Project Milestone 2: Promotional material (25%, practical), Project Milestone 3: Proof of concept (50%, practical). Evidence: machine-learning-ai 0.90 "intuitive understanding of the foundations of Machine Learning".

modules.title: Space Mining
modules.description: The use of space resources will transform human space exploration and create a new economy. In this module, you will explore the legal, technical and economic basis for resource use in space. You will be introduced to the potential target resources (e.g., oxygen), consider the legal aspects of using space resources, and propose a space resource extraction operation. The economic case for your proposed operation will be determined. You will address the challenges of developing new technology for space as well as the potential crossover into terrestrial resource use. This module will teach you to evaluate critically the feasibility of space mining from a legal, technical and economic perspective. You will learn about current activity in this field, using this knowledge to identify limitations in technology, and to propose creative solutions. This module will encourage discussion within and between groups, and you will communicate outcomes to students and experts in the field.
learningOutcomes: Evaluate critically the feasibility of space mining from a legal, technical and economic perspective.
Identify limitations in knowledge and technology and propose creative solutions.
Communicate effectively the outcomes as a group to other students and experts.
Reflect on the potential for the transfer of ideas and technology to terrestrial resources.
modules.derivedRationale: An interdisciplinary introduction to the legal, technical and economic basis for using resources in space. Student groups propose a space resource extraction operation, build its economic case and consider links to terrestrial resource use. Published assessment: Legal Framework document - short written document submitted as a group (30%, coursework), nteractive Poster Presentation submitted as a group (70%, practical). Evidence: law-ip 0.53 "consider the legal aspects of using space resources"; finance-economics 0.53 "The economic case for your proposed operation will be determined.".

modules.title: Virtual Reality: from Concept to Creation
modules.department: I-Explore (Centre for Higher Education Research and Scholarship)
modules.description: In this module you will explore various Virtual Reality applications before creating your own simple Virtual Reality experience relating to your Imperial College student experience. You will work within a multidisciplinary group of students and specialise in the development area of your interest, e.g. user experience/interaction design, graphics, or coding. By the end of the module, you will have enhanced your collaboration, project management, and technical skills and developed a unique Virtual Reality experience.
learningOutcomes: Critically reflect on the strengths and limitations of Virtual Reality for different applications.
Identify and apply the key elements that contribute to a high-quality Virtual Reality experience, focusing on the design of graphics, interactivity and user experience.
Apply basic technical skills and creative approaches in your chosen area of design to help create a component of a Virtual Reality experience.
Plan, manage and execute a Virtual Reality project by defining the scope, breaking down tasks, and adhering to a project timeline.
Work effectively in a multidisciplinary team, negotiating responsibilities and using everyone’s skills to achieve an inventive, common goal.
modules.derivedRationale: Students explore Virtual Reality applications, then work in multidisciplinary groups to design and build a simple VR experience about the Imperial student experience. Each student specialises in an area such as UX/interaction design, graphics or coding while practising project management and teamwork. Published assessment: Group presentation (50%, coursework), Individual journal (50%, coursework). Evidence: creative-arts-design 0.60 "user experience/interaction design, graphics".

modules.title: Management and Decision-Making: Making Smart Decisions
modules.description: The module is designed to equip you to make effective decisions in a wide variety of contexts. The primary context will be in the workplace, whether that be in the private, public or third sector, including government. Many of the methods covered will also be of service in your private lives. Emphasis will be given to broad approaches to decision making, such as Systems Thinking, the PROACT method and understanding common psychological biases in decision making. This will enable you to be intelligent about the process by which decisions are arrived at. In addition, several central decision-making tools will be explained and evaluated, which can support effective decision making within the framework of a well-designed decision process.
learningOutcomes: Select and use appropriate systems methods, to address complex issues.
Select and apply appropriate decision-support tools.
Critically evaluate alternative solutions and strategies for addressing complex problems.
Integrate concepts and ideas from your wider knowledge and viewpoints in a coherent fashion, to address real world problems.
Undertake independent, critically-analytical and reflexive research.
modules.derivedRationale: An introduction to making effective decisions in workplace and personal contexts, covering Systems Thinking, the PROACT method, and psychological biases in decision making. It also explains and evaluates core decision-support tools within a well-designed decision process. Published assessment: Individual written assignment (500 words) (20%, coursework), Individual written assignment (500 words) (20%, coursework), Individual coursework project (2,500 words) (60%, coursework). Evidence: no topic reaches 0.5. Capped at 0.45 for lack of a verbatim quote: management-leadership.

modules.title: Global Economics
modules.description: Global economics is a key contemporary topic, which also bears on a range of pressing political, social and environmental issues. This module provides a comprehensive treatment of the key contemporary issues in global economics and the leading models deployed by global economics institutions such as the WTO, United Nations, IMF and World Bank, as well as by global companies. It will equip you with the conceptual tools to analyse global economic environment of business, both from the corporate and public policy perspectives. The module also provides an opportunity to conduct policy analysis of a global economic issue.
learningOutcomes: Explain the key issues in global economics.
Apply economic analysis tools to a rapidly-changing landscape of international business, and produce recommendations for business strategy.
Apply theory and principles to analyse a key policy issue, and produce a reasoned recommendation for policy intervention.
Present individual work to peers and respond to constructive feedback from facilitator and other learners.
modules.derivedRationale: Introduces key issues in global economics and the models used by institutions such as the WTO, IMF and World Bank. Students apply economic tools to analyse the international business environment and a policy issue, producing strategy and policy recommendations. Published assessment: Group presentation (10 min) and participation in a classroom debate on a specific global economics issue. Group report (12-15 slides). (40%, practical), Individual report (two pages) analysing a global economic environment for a selected company, with a critical review of business strategy options. (30%, coursework), Individual report, submitted as a six-slide deck following a given template, on global economic risks and regulation for a selected area of technology. Topic selected by yourself and approved by module leader. (30%, coursework). Evidence: finance-economics 0.90 "key contemporary issues in global economics and the leading models deployed by global economics institutions"; policy-ethics 0.53 "conduct policy analysis of a global economic issue".

modules.title: History of Science, Technology and Industry
modules.description: This innovative module situates the histories of science, technology and industry within global history, from ancient times to the present day. The concepts of historical time, social and economic development, and even progress, will be examined throughout. Continuity, change and the diffusion of knowledge and practices are central themes. We will cover a variety of activities, such as innovation, research, development, production, distribution, maintenance, and disposal. In so doing, we’ll draw on a diverse array of historical sources and research gathered around themes such as power, control, empire, (de)globalisation, autarchy, logistics, gender, organisation, and work. The module considers older social science thinkers such as Marx, Weber, and Foucault, as well as more recent commentators.
learningOutcomes: Examine key concepts across the discipline of history of science and technology.
Explore concepts using self-directed primary and secondary research.
Integrate concepts studied, research, and feedback received.
Communicate relevant academic concepts and findings in at least two formats.
modules.derivedRationale: A humanities module placing the history of science, technology and industry in global context from antiquity to today. It examines themes such as progress, power, empire, globalisation, gender and work, using primary sources and social thinkers like Marx, Weber and Foucault. Published assessment: Written task (1,200-1,500 words). (30%, coursework), Individual presentation (5 minutes). (15%, practical), Written task (1,500-2,000 words). (55%, coursework). Evidence: history-philosophy 0.95 "situates the histories of science, technology and industry within global history".

modules.title: Philosophy of Mind
modules.description: The module will explore a range of topics in the philosophy of mind, such as the nature of consciousness and thought, the nature of human action and the problem of determinism, the relation between mind (or mental phenomena) and body (or physical phenomena), and the possibility of artificial intelligence. You will gain a deeper understanding of the interplay between philosophical research in these areas and research across a broad range of scientific disciplines, such as neuroscience, life sciences, medicine and computing. By comparing the work of thinkers as diverse as Dennett, Davidson, Putnam, the Churchlands, Fodor, Ryle, Wittgenstein and Heidegger, you will encounter and critically evaluate the cutting edge of modern thinking about the mind, and the issues that must be resolved before embarking on any scientific exploration of the mind.
learningOutcomes: Analyse the structure of some of the major debates within the philosophy of mind.
Communicate verbally, and in writing, the contrasting arguments in the philosophy of mind.
Use creativity and innovation in approaching practical and conceptual problems.
Evaluate and analyse the relevance of complex conceptual issues to your area of degree study.
Select and use a range of sources to critically evaluate and compare the merits of philosophical positions through independent research.
modules.derivedRationale: An introduction to philosophy of mind covering consciousness, thought, action and determinism, the mind-body relation and the possibility of artificial intelligence. It compares major thinkers and links philosophical debates to neuroscience, medicine and computing. Published assessment: 1,500-2,000 word essay, due after the end of autumn term (40%, coursework), 1,500-2,000 word essay, due after the end of spring term (60%, coursework). Evidence: history-philosophy 0.95 "The module will explore a range of topics in the philosophy of mind"; psychology-behaviour 0.50 "the nature of consciousness and thought".

modules.title: Psychology of Performance
modules.description: Do you want to perform at your best? To understand how the greats in business, science, music, sport, medicine, theatre, and countless areas achieve what they achieve? This module will lead you through the latest science examining what it means to perform at the highest level. Looking across disciplines, we will examine the psychology behind leadership, teamwork, motivation, creativity and, very importantly, the psychology of relating to self. We will question whether 10,000 hours of practice is really all it takes to become an expert. We will explore how performance is assessed and valued, and how unconscious biases can affect judges. We will confront the dreaded stage-fright, and how it can be managed. Throughout the module, you will be given the opportunity to experience and reflect on your own performance.
learningOutcomes: Critically evaluate the efficacy of, and scientific evidence underpinning, approaches to performance in your domain.
Compare your areas of performance with others, assessing parallels and differences.
Plan concrete steps to enhance your own performance (including communication and collaboration), based on evidence and best practice.
Design and produce high-impact individual and team performance.
modules.derivedRationale: An interdisciplinary look at the psychology of high performance, covering leadership, teamwork, motivation, creativity, expertise, bias in judging and stage-fright. Students reflect on their own performance and plan evidence-based ways to improve it. Published assessment: Group presentation (15 minutes) (40%, coursework), Reflective commentary (1,800-2,000 words) (60%, coursework). Evidence: psychology-behaviour 0.92 "the latest science examining what it means to perform at the highest level".

modules.title: Science, Policy and Power
modules.description: With guest lecturers from Silicon Valley, politics, think tanks and activist groups, this module explores the intersection between science and policy using multidisciplinary methods. We explore the question of why policy does not always ‘follow the science’ using case studies where science and policy interact such as abortion law, stem cell research, AI development and climate change, looking at the balance of power between the media, public opinion, social norms, and scientific evidence. We also take a deep dive into innovation policy. How do governments and companies foster innovation in science and technology? What is the secret sauce that has made Silicon Valley so successful? This module is taught interactively, requiring students to be engaged and active throughout, whether verbally or in a support role. Two sessions are completely student led.
learningOutcomes: Appreciate the role played by social and ethical values, alongside scientific evidence, in evidence-based policy making.
Use self-directed primary and secondary research, to inform debate on key science funding issues.
Summarise complex scientific research and adapt it to the needs of policy makers.
Analyse science policy topics and persuasively communicate complex concepts.
modules.derivedRationale: An interactive I-Explore module on how science and policy interact, using case studies such as abortion law, stem cell research, AI and climate change to examine why policy doesn't always follow the evidence. It also looks at innovation policy and what made Silicon Valley successful, with guest speakers and student-led sessions. Published assessment: Science briefing (1,000 words) (30%, coursework), Analytical essay (2,000 words) (50%, coursework), Module performance (20%, practical). Evidence: policy-ethics 0.90 "this module explores the intersection between science and policy using multidisciplinary methods"; entrepreneurship-innovation 0.50 "innovation policy".
